content.title: MLB top prospect Konnor Griffin agrees to team-record 9-year contract with Pirates
content.text: Less than a week after making his major-league debut, MLB’s No. 1 prospect Konnor Griffin signed a team record nine-year extension with the Pittsburgh Pirates, giving the team a potential franchise anchor into the mid-2030s.The deal, which league sources confirmed to The Athletic is for $140 million, could be worth up to $150 million with performance escalators. The structure of the deal is as follows – Griffin receives a $12 million signing bonus ($5 million up front and $3.5 million in each of the next two years) with salaries of $1 million in 2026, $2 million in 2027 and $4 million in 2028. He’ll make $6 million in 2029, $12.5 million in 2030 and $21 million in 2031, which likely would have been his final year before free agency. He will earn $26.5 million in 2032 and $27 million in each of the final two years of the deal. It does not include deferrals, opt-out clauses or options.Shortly after the team announced the extension Wednesday morning, Griffin was flanked by Pirates owner Bob Nutting and general manager Ben Cherington at a news conference in PNC Park, where he was met with applause from a contingent that included his teammates, the Pirates’ coaching and performance staff, as well as his wife, parents, brother and father-in-law.“Nine years is a long time,” Nutting said. “I did jot down that it’s 1,458 games. That’s a long time. It’s a real commitment. I could not be more pleased.”Should Griffin, who turns 20 on April 24, play the majority of those contests, he’d be approaching the top 12 in career games for the franchise by the time he becomes eligible for free agency entering his age-29 season in 2035.Cherington noted that one of Griffin’s concerns during the extension negotiations, which transpired throughout the spring, was how established teammates might feel about an unproven player receiving such a significant deal. The show of support in the room, which included several veterans introducing themselves to Griffin’s parents afterwards, seemed to answer that question.“It’s funny, what Ben brought up in the press conference about what would the teammates think about it,” said reigning National League Cy Young Award winner Paul Skenes, whose arrival in Pittsburgh in May 2024 was met with a similar level of hype. “Everybody’s just ecstatic for him. I think it’s funny.“That’s pretty much the only thing he’s done so far that shows he’s 19 years old. It’s not a stupid question or anything; it was just not having been in a big-league clubhouse at the time he asked that. He got the deal that he deserved, and he’s going to be the face of the team for a while.”Griffin is a five-tool phenom who could be the sport’s most exciting prospect since Mike Trout. Griffin’s arrival late last week, in which he became the youngest Pirates player to hit safely in his debut since the late Hall of Famer Bill Mazeroski in 1956, applied the accelerator on what Nutting called “a foot-on-the-gas year” for the club.Your browser does not support the video tag.While the Pirates front office has attempted to tamp down expectations for the teenager, Griffin’s ceiling conjures incredible hope for a fan base desperate for a return to relevance. The Pirates have reached the postseason just three times since 1992, and since Barry Bonds left the franchise after that season, they’ve had only one other NL MVP: Andrew McCutchen.When the Pirates promoted Griffin to the majors, they did so believing that even if he struggles offensively, he’ll still be an upgrade thanks to his speed and defense. So far, that has been true. With game-changing speed and smooth moves at shortstop, Griffin has generated highlights even as he has been slow to get going at the plate, batting 3-for-17 through five games.Griffin is the latest in a series of early extensions. Recently, the Seattle Mariners signed shortstop prospect Colt Emerson to an eight-year, $95 million contract — the largest deal given to a player who has yet to make his MLB debut — and the Milwaukee Brewers inked minor-league shortstop Cooper Pratt, a lower-ranked prospect, to an eight-year, $51 million contract with two option years.For the Pirates, Griffin’s deal marks an unprecedented commitment. Even for a small-market franchise that views early-career extensions — such as the ones signed by McCutchen, Starling Marte, Gregory Polanco, Bryan Reynolds, Ke’Bryan Hayes and Mitch Keller — as vital to its ability to contend, the Pirates had never given out a contract worth more than Reynolds’ $106.75 million extension before Griffin arrived.The sides seemed to be headed for an agreement before Griffin’s call-up was announced Thursday. When Griffin debuted the next day, neither Griffin nor Nutting directly addressed extension talks reported by ESPN, likely because of MLB’s Prospect Promotion Incentive. The program encourages clubs to bring top-100 prospects to the big leagues early by rewarding them with a draft pick based on the player’s finish in major awards voting.To be eligible for a PPI selection, the team must call up the player within the first two weeks of the start of the regular season — which the Pirates didn’t do with Skenes, who debuted May 11, 2024 — and must not sign him to a multiyear extension before his debut.By waiting until after Griffin’s promotion to formalize the extension, the Pirates will receive a PPI pick after the first round if Griffin wins NL Rookie of the Year or finishes in the top three in NL MVP voting.“This is a place I want to be for a long time,” Griffin said Wednesday. “It finally got done in the past few days, and I’m super glad to be part of this organization for a long time.”Additional reporting by The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal
